newsitem.title: GREECE: Salomon cuts earnings estimate for Bank of Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Salomon cuts earnings estimate for Bank of Cyprus.

text.p: Salomon Brothers issued a hold rating for shares of Bank of Cyprus citing disappointing 1996 earnings and a weakened tourism outlook. It also lowered its 1997-98 earnings estimates for the bank.
"Recent political and social tension between Cyprus' Greek and Turkish communities weakens the tourism outlook, forcing us to cut our 1997-98 estimates," it said in a company report.
Bank of Cyprus 1996 earnings grew 5.4 percent to 24.2 million Cyprus pounds against a projected rise of nearly 10 percent.

Political tensions which have added to an already soft tourism season are likely to continue into 1997 as Cyprus prepares for presidential elections in February 1998 and attempts to gain full EU membership.

"Tourism is the prime source of foreign exchange for the island and a dominant contributor to GDP -- 22 percent in 1995. It is also the backbone of real estate prices which are a source of concern to us," said analyst Inigo Lecubarri in a company report.
Salomon shaved its earnings per share (EPS) estimates from C0.3 to C0.24 for 1997 and C0.26 for 1998 but found Bank of Cyprus' convertible bond attractive.

"The 6.75 percent C50 million convertible of October 1996 will continue to perform as an alternative to an Ecu bond, based on its superior 6.6 percent yield to maturity and on the back of further C/Ecu exchange strength," Salomon said.
Expansion into Greece and the local currency remained the main investment attractions.

"The Bank of Cyprus' ability to expand profitability into the public sector-dominated Greek market is the largest growth opportunity available and we would view a strategic acquisition to supplement organic growth a plus," it said.
Three branch openings took place in 1996 and five additions are budgeted for this year.

The Cyprus pound rate has been tracking the Ecu in preparation for full EU membership. Yet Cyprus pound interest rates are significantly higher than Ecu rates and speculators have been prevented from taking full advantage of this by forex controls.
If the controls were relaxed the Cyprus pound would likely appreciate.

Bank of Cyprus shares have slightly outperformed the market since October 1996. However, in absolute terms the shares have fallen around 5.0 percent at a time when Europe's emerging markets were soaring, Salomon said.

"We would be more confident buying the shares at around C2.9 as at the current 1997 P/E of 13.3 times they look fully valued," the report said, seeing no dividend increase in store as the payout ratio of 72 percent was high.
"However, the current 5.5 percent high dividend yield should be a clear support for the stock." --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
